The window was never the problem.

hook: Things a fitter knows that a customer never will
body:
Things a fitter knows that the customer never will:

1. That cill needs a 5mm fall and it will never have one
2. The trickle vent is 40mm from the head and the head is 40mm lower than the drawing
3. That wall is 8mm out of plumb and will stay that way forever
4. The old frame was packed with a rolled-up newspaper from 1994
5. The colour will look different in this light and there is nothing anyone can do about it

Nobody asked. Nobody ever asks. We just know.

body:

The customer will find the difference. In eight years. On a Tuesday. Quietly.

hook: Cill projection: the number nobody ever agrees on
body:
65mm is standard.
75mm is better in the rain.
85mm is what your dad’s has got.

Then you get to the brickwork, and the brickwork has been repointed twice since 1974 and the face is now 12mm further out than the drawing, so your 65mm cill is now a 53mm cill, and now it is not standard and not better in the rain, it is just wet.

Standardise your cill projection. Write it on the job. Then argue about it once, in writing, forever.

A 45° canted bay loses about 30% of its glass to sightlines.

A 30° bay loses about 17%.

It was always going to be bespoke. It was always going to have a drawing. Have the drawing before the customer picks the tile.

hook: Turn a corner: casement, tilt & turn, french, or all three?
body:
Casement: cheapest, opens out, hinges eat clear glass.

Tilt & turn: opens in for cleaning, hinges invisible, hardware costs more.

French: two sashes, no mullion, doubles the sightline risk, best with a shallow reveal.

hook: Five things that turn a good install into a bad one
body:
1. The foam. Too little and it moves, too much and it bows the frame.
2. The fixings. Into the reveal, into solid, never into the old frame.
3. The gaps. If the perimeter gap is not consistent, the sealant tells the truth eventually.
4. The sill. Level, with fall, horned, and cut to the wall not to the paper.
5. The protection. If it isn’t taped, it will be marked. If it isn’t boarded, it will be scratched.

Five things. That is the craft.

Once you see it you cannot unsee it. And you cannot unsee it in the customer’s sitting room either.

And yet. We are all going to try.

hook: What Article 4 actually does (in a way nobody explains it)
body:
Slide 1: Normally, in England, replacing windows in a house is permitted development. No permission. Just do it.

Slide 2: Article 4 takes that right away from you in a specific direction — usually the front — usually to protect a view.

Slide 3: In a conservation area the same applies, and in Scotland since May 2024, prior notification applies to a lot of listed and street-facing windows.

Slide 4: On a listed building you need listed building consent and uPVC is basically never acceptable.

Slide 5: The mistake: finding out all of this after you have surveyed, specified and quoted.

hook: What 100 surveys taught me about UK houses
body:
After a hundred surveys I can tell you these things with confidence:

The drawing is wrong more often than it is right.
The reveal is square about a third of the time.
The lintel is a problem roughly half the time.
Nobody has ever had the cavity filled correctly.
At least one window per job is above a downpipe.
The customer is right about the wall being level about four per cent of the time.

body:
Slide 1: There is a 2mm difference in cavity width, which is a 12% difference in energy loss.

Slide 2: There is argon and there is air, and it is about 15% of the U-value.

Slide 3: There is warm edge and there is aluminium, and it matters at the perimeter, which is where the loss actually is.

Slide 4: There is a coated face and there is a clear face, and it has to go the right way up or it is worse than nothing.

Slide 5: There is no such thing as a standard sealed unit. Ask for the make-up in millimetres and watch what happens.

hook: The window industry has a data problem, not a sales problem
body:
Nobody in UK window manufacturing is short of work.

What they are short of is certainty. Certainty about what was quoted. What was surveyed. What was ordered. What was made. What was delivered. What was paid.

Six organisations, six systems, and one person — usually the most overloaded person in the company — responsible for the integrity of the whole chain.

The remake rate in this industry is a direct, measurable function of how many systems a job passes through. It is not a quality problem. Quality is the best part of this trade. It is a reconciliation problem.

hook: Why we will not publish a customer testimonial
body:
We could have a wall of them tomorrow. That was available to us on day one.

The reason we have not is that every customer we have is a window business, and a window business that publishes its own margin, its own remake rate and its own quoting failures to a software vendor's website has taken a risk it did not need to take.

So we will not ask.

What we will publish instead is four measures: time to quote, remakes, margin held against margin quoted, and re-entries per job. Real businesses, real figures, agreed in writing before anything goes on the site.

We have none of those published yet. Not because we do not track them, but because we do not have permission from the right number of people.

That is a slower way to build trust. It is also the only way that survives a reference call.

hook: Window businesses do not lose money in the factory
body:
They lose it in four places that almost nobody writes down.

One: the survey. An opening comes in 9mm out, it becomes a wedge, a second visit and a morning, and it is absorbed because the quote was a lump sum with a fitting percentage buried inside it.

Two: the office. The specification is re-keyed between systems, and once it is re-keyed it belongs to whoever keyed it last.

Three: the second visit. “Just while you're here” has no scope, no price and no owner, and it is the single most expensive sentence in domestic construction.

Four: delivery. A 2,180mm frame on an unsuitable vehicle becomes two vans, and two vans are rarely in anybody's model.

None of this is a manufacturing problem. The manufacturing in this industry is genuinely world class.

It is a data problem, and data problems are cheap to fix and expensive to ignore.

hook: The spreadsheet is not a cheap version of quoting software
body:
It is a shared, mutable document with no version history, no permissions, no validation and no relationship to anything else in the business.

Every modification overwrites the last. Two people cannot work in it at once. Nothing enforces that a width is a number. Nothing knows that opening W0.2 belongs to a survey that belongs to a job that belongs to a customer.

And the cell that somebody changed last Thursday — the one that moves a casement from 1200 to 1186 — has no record of who changed it, when, or why, and by the time anybody notices, the frame is on a van.

A spreadsheet is a genuinely useful tool. It is a terrible system of record.

The distinction matters because most small businesses have quietly decided that the spreadsheet is the system. It is not the system. It is the place the data goes to get lost.
